issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Description

Evaluate whether June 67B context-extension checkpoints use retained MRCR conversation context when scoring the same final assistant response. The paired evaluator compares `full_context` with `query_only`, scores response-body tokens, and stratifies deterministic bootstrap intervals by needle count and evidence distance.

## Task

An MRCR source document contains two worked examples, a long multi-turn conversation with 2, 4, or 8 relevant facts ("needles"), and a final query. `desired_msg_index` identifies a user request in that conversation; its matching answer is the immediately following assistant message.

Each source row produces two documents with the same final query and gold response:

```text
full_context: two worked examples + target conversation + final query -> gold response
query_only:   two worked examples + final query                       -> gold response
```

The primary two-shot prompt supplies the benchmark's 10-character answer prefix. The evaluator scores only the remaining gold assistant response body. The worked examples, retained conversation, final query, supplied prefix, and EOS are context and receive zero loss. Each condition occupies one unsliced, unpacked sequence.

The paired comparison asks whether retaining the target conversation improves the likelihood of the identical response. Results report `query_only - full_context` NLL and BPB gain, with response-token micro and per-example macro aggregation, sliced by needle count and evidence distance.

### Difference from standard MRCR

Standard OpenAI MRCR gives the model the complete conversation, samples a response, requires the nonce prefix in that response, and grades the generated text with a `SequenceMatcher` similarity score. This experiment instead teacher-forces the gold response and measures its token likelihood twice: once with the target conversation and once without it. The supplied prefix is not scored. The resulting paired NLL/BPB gain is a diagnostic of context use, not an official MRCR generation score, and should not be compared directly with published MRCR scores.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Context gain (`query_only - full_context`) should move from non-positive before extension to positive after 64K/262K adaptation. Fixed qk=1.57 comparisons isolate checkpoint adaptation; qk=1.75 is the deployable final arm.

### Links

- [OpenAI MRCR dataset and task description](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr/tree/f4c69fae7cf81f7ca26b9fee34b392a50f6b8a1d)
- [Research logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/babf963076/.agents/logbooks/paired-mrcr-base-eval.md)
- [Implementation snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/63027b4e72)
- [Final qk1.57 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk157-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)
- [Final qk1.75 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk175-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)

## Results

Context gain is `query_only - full_context`, so positive NLL or BPB gain is beneficial.

| Checkpoint | qk | NLL gain (95% CI) | BPB gain |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| step 141000, pre-extension (8K) | 1.57 | -0.19453 [-0.21900, -0.16930] | -0.05789 |
| step 156000, 64K source | 1.57 | +0.40387 [+0.36399, +0.44537] | +0.12019 |
| step 157000, 262K extension | 1.57 | +1.18860 [+1.14205, +1.23597] | +0.35371 |
| step 157000, deployable arm | 1.75 | +1.26855 [+1.22432, +1.31342] | +0.37751 |

Each checkpoint used the same 299 paired source examples: 598 full-context/query-only condition sequences. Across four checkpoints, this is 1,196 paired checkpoint-example comparisons and 2,392 condition sequences.

Confidence is exploratory because each checkpoint received one evaluation pass over this dataset. One-shot/no-prefix and the full matrix remain untested.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Added a four-condition oracle-normalized measurement before rerunning the 299-example 262K slice.

The conditions form a 2×2 comparison: needles absent/present and distractors absent/present. `needle_only` retains all repeated target-request turns so the ordinal retrieval problem is preserved; `distractor_only` retains the complementary conversation turns. All four conditions score the same response-body tokens.

The headline recovery ratio is `(distractor_only NLL - full_context NLL) / (query_only NLL - needle_only NLL)`, computed as a token-micro ratio of aggregate paired contrasts. A 10,000-sample bootstrap resamples the same four-condition source tuples within needle-count and evidence-distance strata.

The ratio is identifiable only when the isolated-needle gain is at least 0.10 nats/token, its bootstrap lower bound is positive, at least 99% of bootstrap denominators are positive, and no denominator is zero. Before seeing results, the “good enough” gate is a recovery-ratio 95% lower bound of at least 0.80 plus a positive lower bound for distracted needle gain. Needle-count slices must each have positive distracted needle gain; distance slices are descriptive.

Implementation: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/5c32364665

Next: run the pre-extension checkpoint as a memory/artifact probe on `v4-64-cp8-ep4`, then run the remaining three checkpoints if it succeeds.

issues.body:
Some potential improvements we noticed during the hero run rollout.

scatter aggregation:
  - can you run a scatter aggregation step alongside the mappers? for each N map shards finished, read them in and reshuffle/merge the outputs by reduce shard. the inputs should be pre-sorted by target shard, so in theory this can be done with low-memory. this should reduce read traffic by a factor of ~N, and potentially eliminates the external sort we currently do entirely

datafusion as a loading api:
  - supports parquet reading & query push down
  - seems robust from our experience with finelog
  - trivializes a "lite" sql select only API
  - would be nice for library sharing across projects

mapper auto-tuning:
  - choose the number of mappers for the user based on heuristics or dynamically based on observations
  - we have many pipelines that run 10x too slow just because they have fewer mappers than needed
  - combine this with the scatter aggregation to avoid map/reduce shard blowup

better partial recovery:
  - allow recovering a partially complete run
  - for example the zephyr coordinator might write a state record once a minute recording all of the shard state
  - check for this when booting up and reuse it if the ids match

kv-store work scattering:
  - the kv store actors can be used in the some situations to split up imbalanced workloads
  - push the work to the kv store via compute functions

issues.author: wmoss
issues.body:
Iris controller restarts today are driven entirely by `iris cluster controller restart` (see `lib/iris/OPS.md`, `.agents/skills/restart-iris/`) — GCE clusters restart via SSH + `docker restart`, CoreWeave clusters via the Kubernetes API — not by Pulumi. This is an investigation, not a commitment to migrate: the restart flow has safety properties that a naive Pulumi resource-replace would break if not carried over deliberately.

Specifically: the controller keeps local SQLite state plus periodic GCS checkpoints, and restart takes a pre-restart checkpoint and writes a rollout record (image + matching checkpoint ref) so a failed health check can roll back atomically. DB migrations are forward-only and some are destructive, so restoring an old controller image without its paired pre-migration checkpoint breaks. Any Pulumi-driven approach needs to preserve this checkpoint-before-restart / paired-rollback behavior, e.g. by keeping restart-with-rollback as a wrapped CLI step (similar to how `iac.iris.service` wraps a CLI today) rather than modeling the controller as a plain replaceable resource.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Investigation, not a bug fix — no PR. Analysis below; handing off to a human for the migrate/don't-migrate call.

# Research

Confirmed the issue body against the code. `iris cluster controller restart` is a CLI-side choreography around a mechanical platform restart; the safety lives in the CLI, not in the platform primitive.

Forward deploy in [`cli/cluster.py:controller_restart` L1117-1215](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1117-L1215): pre-deploy checkpoint (L1180) → build fresh images (L1182) → write `PENDING` rollout record (L1187) → `restart_controller` (L1199) → on health-check failure `_auto_rollback` to previous image + its pre-deploy checkpoint (L1202) → write `COMMITTED` (L1206). `--rollback` (L1148) reverts to the recorded previous image + checkpoint.

The rollout record is a small state machine in GCS remote state, not in any deploy tool's state; the restarted controller consumes `ROLLBACK_REQUESTED` once on boot and self-clears. Migrations are forward-only and some are destructive, so an old image must boot on its paired pre-migration checkpoint — this is why image and checkpoint are recorded as a pair.

**Relevant code**
- [`cli/cluster.py#L1117`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1117) - restart/rollback choreography (checkpoint, record, restart, auto-rollback)
- [`controller/rollout.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/rollout.py) - `RolloutPhase`/`RolloutRecord`, read/write in GCS remote state
- [`platforms/vm_lifecycle.py#L409`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/vm_lifecycle.py#L409) / [`k8s/controller.py#L517`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L517) - mechanical restart primitives (no safety logic)
- [`controller/migrations/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/migrations) - forward-only, sometimes destructive
- [`iac/iris/service.py#L156-L164`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py#L156-L164) - existing CLI-wrap template to reuse

# Proposed approach

Do **not** model the controller as a plain replaceable Pulumi resource. A resource-replace would tear down and recreate around the restart, bypassing the checkpoint/rollout-record choreography and losing atomic rollback on a bad deploy.

Instead reuse the pattern already in [`iac/iris/service.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py) (and the sibling finelog migration in #7571): wrap `iris cluster controller restart` in a `command.local.Command` component whose `create`/`update` verb runs the restart CLI and whose `delete` is a no-op (or `stop`, deliberately). Key the resource on the controller image tag plus a code hash so a change triggers `update` = restart-with-rollback; a failed health check propagates as a Command error, and the CLI has already auto-rolled-back. The rollout record stays in GCS remote state so `--rollback` keeps working out-of-band from Pulumi state.

Open questions for the human owner:
- Is the goal declarative *drift correction* (Pulumi restarts when image drifts) or just *inventory* (record the controller in the stack without owning restarts)? The wrapper above gives the former; only the latter avoids Pulumi ever triggering a restart.
- How should a Pulumi `up` that fails its health check and auto-rolls-back report to the operator — hard resource failure, or success-with-warning after rollback?
- Interaction with the manual `restart-iris` skill / direct CLI runs: Pulumi must treat an out-of-band restart as convergent, not as drift to undo.

Scope is a new Pulumi component plus wiring — multi-file design work, so leaving implementation to a human per the migration effort in #7571/#7262.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Investigation result: move Iris controller operations under the shared deploy interface, with Pulumi invoking the existing migration-aware restart transaction. Do not make the controller VM or Kubernetes Deployment a plain replaceable Pulumi resource.

Effort: medium, 2026-08-24. I stopped after the current code, linked PRs, Echo history, and Pulumi documentation converged on the same boundary.

### Current Marin context

The new work changes the operator interface, but not Iris's state-safety requirement:

- [#8537](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8537) provides one command tree for Pulumi applications. The executable merged there is `marin-deploy`, so the exact spelling today is `uv run marin-deploy ...`; adding a `deploy` script alias is independent of this design.
- [`controller restart`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1263-L1532) resolves secrets, checkpoints the live controller, builds and pins images, writes `PENDING`, restarts in place, health-checks, and commits or restores the previous image plus checkpoint. The controller [consumes the rollback request once](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/main.py#L51-L85).
- Pulumi [does not automatically roll back a failed update](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/support/faq/infrastructure/#automatic-rollbacks). Finelog therefore captures the active revision outside Pulumi, runs `pulumi up`, restores on failure, and refreshes state ([#7690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7690), [current implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/_k8s.py#L390-L471)). Iris needs that recovery boundary and its additional checkpoint pairing.

### Recommended first migration

1. Add a separate `infra/iris` application project with one stack per controller cluster. This follows the repository rule that application deploy lifecycles stay outside the static `infra/pulumi` substrate project.
2. Add an Iris controller component backed by `command.local.Command`. Its `create` and `update` verbs run the existing `iris cluster controller restart`; removal has no stop/delete verb. Inputs include the cluster, reviewed config hash, working-tree hash, and an explicit deploy generation for a forced same-tree restart. Pulumi's command provider runs `update` when inputs/triggers change instead of replacing the resource ([provider contract](https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/command/api-docs/local/command/)).
3. Add service-specific commands:

   ```text
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollout <cluster>
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollout <cluster> --force
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollback <cluster>
   ```

   `rollback` must call the existing `--rollback` path and use the GCS rollout record. Pulumi history is not a substitute for the recorded image/checkpoint pair. The rollout record remains the recovery source of truth; Pulumi records which reviewed tree/config triggered the transaction.
4. Keep the existing fleet gates: clean/current tree preflight, one cluster at a time, baseline snapshot, five-minute verification, and smoke job. Do not add Iris to the parallel path-triggered deployment matrix in the first change. That matrix cannot currently stop the fleet at the first failed cluster, and GCE restarts also require per-user SSH access.

This stage gives Iris the shared `marin-deploy` UX and Pulumi update/audit surface while preserving the current transaction even when an operator runs `pulumi up` directly.

### Native-resource follow-up

A later CoreWeave-only stage can adopt the non-secret runtime objects into an application stack: ConfigMap, protected PVC, Recreate Deployment, Service, PDB, node-agent DaemonSet, LocalQueue, and priority classes. It should proceed only after the deploy driver is split into prepare/activate/finalize/rollback operations and these conditions are tested:

- no workload mutation before a fresh checkpoint and `PENDING` record;
- every activation or health failure restores the recorded image and checkpoint, waits for `ROLLED_BACK`, then refreshes Pulumi state;
- direct `pulumi up` cannot bypass preparation;
- secret values remain outside Pulumi state;
- controller storage is protected, and GCE application changes never replace the controller VM;
- manual break-glass rollback remains convergent with the next intentional rollout.

Confidence is high for the first migration. Native CoreWeave ownership is feasible with those gates, but it is a separate lifecycle refactor; GCE should continue using the in-place SSH restart mechanism behind the same command.

### Handoff

No PR was opened because this request was an investigation. The next decision is whether to implement the first migration as scoped above and track native CoreWeave resource ownership separately.

issues.author: dbuddha
issues.body:
Hi all, I'm Deepak, a Stanford student, and I've been working on this as my CS221 project. It started from Will's suggestion to begin with the Delphi seed repeats, and from his note in the Nov 2 standup (#11169) that, with loop variance this high, it would help to have documented expected variance so agents know what counts as a regression. Calvin also suggested in #data-mixing that we target fewer evals, possibly one that generalizes well, instead of a big aggregate, so I tested one version of that too. Everything here uses public data, and I'm happy to share more detail on any of it.

## Short version

I measured how much eval scores move between training seeds of the same recipe. I used DataDecide's per-question results (3 seeds per recipe), and the public Delphi seed triples at 1e21 and 1e22, which I scored with Marin's eval suite and the pinned stanford-crfm harness.

The part I think is most useful for Marin is that item-sampling SE is not a good stand-in for seed noise, and it misses in both directions. For soft metrics like gold log-prob or BPB, item SE usually understates seed noise, sometimes several times over. For accuracy it depends on the task: item SE overstates seed noise for HellaSwag and MMLU on DataDecide, and understates it for the DataDecide 10-task average. For Delphi MMLU 0-shot accuracy the ratio is about 1.3, which is within noise of 1 with three seeds. The ratio may also move with scale. For MMLU 0-shot log-prob on Delphi, seed SD is about 4x the item SE at 1e21 and about 1x at 1e22, though with three seeds per scale that change isn't significant (p about 0.1).

On Calvin's suggestion, picking a single eval by SNR went badly. The 10-task average ordered 82% of recipe pairs the same way as at 1B, and the highest-SNR single eval got 57%. The best single eval in hindsight tied the average, but it is the best of 20 and changes with the decision scale, and on Marin's swarms (comment below) the best single task in hindsight trails the aggregate.

I also tried to forecast seed noise as a power law in compute, and that did not work.

## Why this matters for the current gates

Several gates set thresholds from item SEs or fixed bands, and the ones that use seed replicates have only a few:

- The release tie rule in #10197 uses unpaired item SEs. There is an open question there about paired SEs. For picking one fixed release checkpoint, item SE may be the right noise. Seed noise matters when the call is about a recipe.
- Data Belay (#11582) uses 3 seeds per arm with a 1% floor, and suggests pooling the control's seed variance across rungs.
- The loop presets in #10740 compare against a few control replicates.
- #11177 notes that paired-item variance is unmeasured.
- #10804 notes that interval calibration for Mini840 and Micro210 is not established.
- Belay (#9451) uses a fixed 0.005 band.
- Ladder forecasts like #10753 seem to fit one run per rung, so seed noise at the small rungs would go straight into the extrapolation.

#5247 is the closest earlier work on choosing a useful set of evals. It measured noise from 10 repeat runs at 300M and ended on choosing, for each task, the smooth proxy with the highest SNR. Result 2 tests a different rule, keeping one eval chosen by SNR across all tasks, which is closer to the fewer-evals idea.

## What I measured

**DataDecide** (`allenai/DataDecide-eval-instances`, revision `23f3b2e`). 10 OLMES tasks, using each task's primary metric and the gold-choice log-prob per character. I used two subsets:

- Eval selection (Results 2 and 3): 24 of the 25 recipes, 3 seeds each, read at the last step that every recipe and seed shares: 150M at 37,500, 300M at 45,000 and 1B at 69,369. These are about 98% of training for the two smaller sizes, and final for 1B. I left out `dolma1.7-no-math-no-code`, because its 1B seed 4 only has a checkpoint at 57,500.
- Noise forecast and the DataDecide ratios (Results 1 and 4): 5 recipes (`c4`, `dclm-baseline`, `dolma1.7`, `falcon-with-cc`, `fineweb-edu`) at all five sizes, each read at the last step its three seeds share. For 530M and 750M that step is at 89% and 43% of the schedule.

**Delphi on Marin's suite.**

- Checkpoints: `delphi-1e21-3.4Bparams-46.3Btokens` and `delphi-1e22-9.7Bparams-160Btokens`, default seed plus seeds 42 and 62746.
- Tasks: `mmlu_sl_verb` 0-shot and 5-shot, and the `logprob_gsm8k_5shot` and `logprob_humaneval_10shot` configs from [`experiments/exp1337_eval_suite.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f08afdb5ec98c742c06a5e72d9a987aa9db1e450/experiments/exp1337_eval_suite.py) (since removed from main in #6633).
- Harness: `stanford-crfm/lm-evaluation-harness@d5e3391f` with the HF backend on one H100, BF16 weights, batch size auto. I logged per-sample results.
- I recreated the two logprob tasks as YAML with the same fields as the suite, except that I requested perplexity instead of `bpb` so the harness would log each document's log-likelihood. I computed BPB per document from that log-likelihood and the target's bytes, which matches the suite's per-document mean.

**Delphi GSM8K rollouts.** The per-seed rollouts that `tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws` (commit `c0490e5`) published: 256 problems for every seeded Delphi budget, with 32 rollouts per hint level and 64 unhinted. That repo has no license file, so I only report aggregates from it.

## Results

### 1. Seed noise vs item SE on Delphi

Each value is seed SD divided by item SE. Seed SD is taken across the three seeds, and item SE comes from the default seed (micro averages).

| Metric | 1e21 | 1e22 |
|---|---:|---:|
| MMLU 0-shot accuracy | 1.28 | 1.35 |
| MMLU 0-shot gold-choice log-prob | 4.10 | 1.03 |
| MMLU 5-shot accuracy | 0.71 | 0.69 |
| MMLU 5-shot gold-choice log-prob | 1.99 | 1.83 |
| GSM8K 5-shot BPB | 2.61 | 0.56 |
| HumanEval 10-shot BPB (see the fidelity note) | 0.05 | 1.02 |

DataDecide (the 5-recipe subset) shows a similar split. For accuracy on HellaSwag and MMLU, seed SD is 0.3x to 0.75x the item SE, but for BoolQ accuracy it is 4x to 9x. For gold log-prob on ARC-Easy, HellaSwag and MMLU it is 1.1x to 12x, and it is largest at 530M and 750M, whose checkpoints come before the end of the LR schedule. Across all 10 tasks, gold log-prob ranges from 0.3x (WinoGrande) to 88x (BoolQ).

So I don't think one rule of thumb works. An item-SE tie rule is on the cautious side for some accuracy metrics, too willing to call differences real for others, and too willing for most soft metrics. These ratios are exploratory, not part of a preregistered test.

### 2. Does one eval recover the winner? (Calvin's suggestion)

Setup: I picked a recipe using results at 300M (or 150M), and counted it correct if it matched the sign of the 3-seed mean macro accuracy at 1B, over all 276 recipe pairs. SNR is the spread of recipe means divided by the pooled seed SD, measured at 150M only. I wrote the plan down before computing any of these numbers.

| Decide at | Seeds per recipe | 10-task average | Highest-SNR single eval (HellaSwag gold log-prob) | Best single eval in hindsight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 300M | 1 | 0.822 | 0.570 | CSQA accuracy, 0.819 |
| 300M | 3 | 0.848 | 0.569 | CSQA accuracy, 0.848 |
| 150M | 1 | 0.797 | 0.600 | OpenBookQA gold log-prob, 0.786 |
| 150M | 3 | 0.808 | 0.605 | CSQA accuracy, 0.815 |

At 300M with one seed per recipe, the bootstrap 95% interval for "single eval minus average" is -0.447 to -0.048. The interval resamples recipes, 2,000 draws. At 150M the intervals cross zero (-0.398 to +0.030 with one seed per recipe, -0.410 to +0.019 with three). PIQA accuracy actually points the wrong way (0.44).

HellaSwag gold log-prob separates recipes very consistently, but in a different order from the broad target. Every eval here runs on the same training runs, so the average adds eval compute but no extra runs. My read is that low noise alone isn't enough to pick one eval. CSQA accuracy tied the average here, but I only know that in hindsight, and it gets 0.73 when the decision is made at 150M.

One fair objection is that the 1B target is accuracy, which is noisy. So I also scored the same 300M picks (one seed per recipe) against smooth 1B targets. This check is exploratory:

| Picked at 300M | 1B average accuracy (target above) | 1B average gold log-prob | 1B HellaSwag gold log-prob |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| HellaSwag gold log-prob (highest SNR) | 0.570 | 0.510 | 0.941 |
| Average of the 10 gold log-probs | 0.844 | 0.844 | 0.466 |
| Average of the 10 accuracies | 0.822 | 0.779 | 0.435 |

The two broad 1B targets agree on 90% of pairs, and the smooth one doesn't rescue the single eval. HellaSwag gold log-prob tracks HellaSwag itself across scale (94%), so here the problem looks like breadth more than smoothness. On Marin's swarms some single tasks also reorder between rungs (comment below). Averaging the smooth proxies did best for both broad targets.

### 3. Tie rules on the aggregate

Decisions at 300M with one seed per recipe, on the 10-task average:

| Rule | Share of pairs it calls | Accuracy when it calls |
|---|---:|---:|
| Unpaired item-SE rule (1.96 x hypot of item SEs) | 0.75 | 0.886 |
| Fixed 1% relative band | 0.89 | 0.852 |
| Seed-calibrated: seed variance = 2.69 x item variance, fit at 150M only | 0.61 | 0.919 |

The seed-calibrated rule is the item-SE rule with the threshold widened by sqrt(2.69) = 1.64, so it is stricter by construction, and a higher hit rate on its calls is expected. It gets fewer pairs right overall (56% of all pairs vs 67%). The useful part is the 2.69 itself: on a fixed benchmark, a 1.96 item-SE threshold is only 1.2 seed SDs here, so under a normal approximation two equal recipes would be called different about 23% of the time instead of 5%.

### 4. Forecasting seed noise across scale (negative result)

I fit log seed variance as a power law in compute on the smaller sizes, and scored the forecast on held-out larger ones. On DataDecide (the 5-recipe subset, fit on 150M to 530M, 1B held out), it beat the best simple baseline in only 4 of 20 task and metric groups. A simpler rule did better there (seed variance as a fixed multiple of item variance), winning 11 of 20, though only 5 of 20 at 750M.

On the Delphi GSM8K rollouts, both lost to the best baseline at 1e21 and 1e22. Seed noise on the main hinted metric dropped from 2.8 points at 1e21 to 0.26 points at 1e22, while the power law expected it to keep growing. So I don't think a compute-only law is the right way to set thresholds per rung, at least with 3 seeds, and a ratio fit at one scale may not carry to another.

### Smaller things

- Scoring the same 1e21 default weights twice (first pass) gave identical per-question values, so eval nondeterminism isn't behind the seed differences.
- Between pairs of Delphi seeds, 39% to 65% of MMLU answers change, and correctness flips on 24% to 34% of questions.
- On MMLU 0-shot, a question that flips between seeds at 1e21 is only a little more likely to flip at 1e22 (0.49 vs 0.40, phi 0.10). This one is exploratory.
- As a sanity check, refitting Chinchilla Approach 2 on `delphi-blog-data` reproduces Delphi's published optimal model sizes within about 3%. Fit only up to 3e20, it predicts the released losses at 1e21, 1e22 and 1e23 within 0.3%.

## Fidelity against Marin's published default-seed numbers

I averaged every metric per subject, because that is what matches Marin's published numbers. The fork's group value does the same for `choice_logprob`, but weights accuracy by subject size (0.2700 at 1e21 and 0.4110 at 1e22), so its group accuracy won't match the blog at 1e22. Each pair is this run vs `delphi-blog-data`.

| Metric | 1e21 | 1e22 |
|---|---|---|
| MMLU 0-shot accuracy | 0.2703 vs 0.2710 | 0.4191 vs 0.4192 |
| MMLU 0-shot `choice_logprob` | -1.51430 vs -1.51440 | -1.29253 vs -1.29259 |
| MMLU 5-shot accuracy | 0.2783 vs 0.2751 | 0.4675 vs 0.4699 |
| MMLU 5-shot `choice_logprob` | -1.48028 vs -1.47965 | -1.21529 vs -1.21474 |
| GSM8K 5-shot BPB | 0.5637 vs 0.5631 | 0.4391 vs 0.4384 |
| HumanEval 10-shot BPB | 0.6147 vs 0.5195 | 0.4819 vs 0.4136 |

HumanEval doesn't match, and I haven't found why yet. It isn't truncation: the longest context is 2,669 tokens. GSM8K matches with the same BPB formula. If anyone knows how the HumanEval numbers in the Delphi post were produced (backend, tokenization of the solution, few-shot source), I'd love to fix it. Until then I'm treating the HumanEval rows as this harness only.

## Evidence and setup

- Command for the first pass: `lm_eval --model hf --model_args pretrained=<checkpoint>,dtype=bfloat16 --tasks mmlu_sl_verb,logprob_gsm8k_5shot,logprob_humaneval_10shot --include_path <tasks dir> --batch_size auto --log_samples --output_path <out>`. The 5-shot pass used `--tasks mmlu_sl_verb --num_fewshot 5`.
- Versions: lm-eval 0.4.9.1 from the fork, transformers 4.57.6, datasets 3.6.0, on the `runpod/pytorch:1.0.2-cu1281-torch280-ubuntu2404` image with one H100 80GB.
- Delphi revisions:
  - 1e21: `37bd7d2`, `cf238a2` (seed 42), `63f48f1` (seed 62746).
  - 1e22: `8ac3229`, `fb30c1b` (seed 42), `fcc5ce0` (seed 62746).
  - Blog data: `78f8e0c`.
- Cost: 13 runs (6 checkpoints x 2 passes, plus one A/A repeat) in 4.36 billed H100-hours, including installs and downloads.
  - A 3.4B first pass took about 7 minutes of eval time.
  - MMLU 5-shot is 41.9M tokens per checkpoint, and 0-shot is 7.3M.
- Process: I committed the plans for the forecast (Result 4) and the eval selection (Results 2 and 3) before scoring the held-out data. The ratio tables, the target check in Result 2 and the flip analysis are exploratory. I can share the notes, the per-question outputs and the scripts.

## Limits

- Only 3 seeds per configuration, so a single seed SD is uncertain by roughly 0.5x to 6x (95%), and I lean on pooling across recipes and metrics.
- Two families (OLMo-style DataDecide up to 1B, and Delphi). Delphi has no recipe pairs, so the decision-accuracy results come from DataDecide only.
- These are pretraining log-likelihood evals. Loop evals generate answers, and an earlier version of the #10740 description reported 210 of 1,500 task scores changing between two greedy passes of the same weights, so the numbers here may not carry over. The method should.
- The 1e21 W&B configs set trainer seeds 0, 42 and 62746 with `data_seed` null, and Levanter then derives the data order from the trainer seed. So each seed changes both initialization and data order, and I can't say which one drives the noise. The 1e21 default run also used a different code commit (`de20b33`) from the two seed runs (`67099b9`). I haven't checked the 1e22 configs.

## Asks

- **@Calvin-Xu**: to test the eval-selection result on Marin's own mixtures, I'd need the same mixtures run at a small and a larger rung with the same evals. The public `grug-moe-mix-swarm` has 10 seed repeats of a proportional mix at d512, and 10 runs of a proportional mix at d768 (their names show different loader settings too), but the two use different stores, and I couldn't match any d512 design to a d768 one. Do you know if a two-rung set like that exists?
- **@penfever**: would a per-metric seed-noise table be useful for the tie rule in #10197, maybe with a separate threshold for soft metrics? I realize it matters more for recipe calls than for picking a fixed release checkpoint.
- **@Helw150** and **@RohithKuditipudi**: the 20 seed checkpoints from #10555 (blocked by #10758), or just their per-question eval outputs, would let me fit noise for multiple-choice metrics across eleven budgets instead of two. Even 3e19 and 3e20 would help.
- And if anyone is already looking at seed noise on the Delphi ladder, I'd really like to compare notes rather than duplicate it

Thanks for reading, and for putting all of this out in the open

_Edited Nov 21: fixed the accuracy claim (item SE understates seed noise for some accuracy metrics too), described the 5-recipe DataDecide subset, and corrected the rollout counts, the budget count, the MMLU aggregation note, the Result 3 reading and two links. Added #10753, the #5247 context and an exploratory target check in Result 2._

_Edited Nov 26: corrected how I described #5247 (it picks a smooth proxy per task), softened the hindsight-eval and Delphi-ratio claims, which three seeds can't support, added the 150M intervals, tightened the #10804 and #10753 descriptions, and noted the one field I changed in the task configs. The swarm results are in the comment below._

comments.author: Calvin-Xu
comments.body:
> Do you know if a two-rung set like that exists?

Our data mixing swarms are probably useful:

> The same 280 mixtures over 39 data buckets (238 sampled designs, 39 single-bucket removals, and 3 baselines) were trained at three settings: Llama 160M/1.2B, Llama 200M/6B, and Qwen3 360M/1.6B (about 3e18 FLOPs). Each setting also has 10 repeats of the proportional mixture. Every run has BPB on the same 58 tasks: the 7 Uncheatable Eval corpora and the 51 OlmoBaseEval Easy tasks.
> 
> | Setting | Repeat SD, Uncheatable BPB | Repeat SD, OBE Easy mean BPB | Spearman with 360M/1.6B (Uncheatable / OBE Easy) |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | Llama 160M/1.2B | 0.0011 | 0.0054 | 0.92 / 0.85 |
> | Llama 200M/6B | 0.0012 | 0.0035 | 0.62 / 0.55 |
> | Qwen3 360M/1.6B | 0.0009 | 0.0038 | |
> 
> Repeat SDs come from the 10 proportional repeats; the Spearman correlations are over the 238 sampled designs.
> 
> The 871 checkpoints are public on Hugging Face as `Calvin-Xu/mariner-swarm-llama-160m-1p2b`, `Calvin-Xu/mariner-swarm-llama-200m-6b`, and `Calvin-Xu/mariner-swarm-qwen3-360m-1p6b`.

The same dataset has a ladder with more scales and fewer recipes: proportional, UniMax, and MARINER's and Olmix's proposals at 3e18, 2e19, 3e20, and 1e21 FLOPs, though only proportional at 3e18 have seed repeats.

comments.author: dbuddha
comments.body:
Thanks @Calvin-Xu for sharing those!! I committed the test plan before opening any BPB columns and then ran it once. It decides on Llama 160M/1.2B and scores against Llama 200M/6B over the 238 sampled mixtures, one run each. 200M/6B has 1.3x the parameters, 5x the tokens and half the peak learning rate, so it tests repetition as much as scale. A rule gets a pair right if it orders the two mixtures the same way 200M/6B does, and a task's SNR is its SD across the 238 designs over its SD across the 10 proportional repeats at 160M. The numbers below are decision accuracy, the share of the 28,203 pairs a rule gets right, so 0.5 is a coin flip.

| Picked at 160M/1.2B | Decision accuracy against OBE Easy mean BPB at 200M/6B | Decision accuracy against Uncheatable BPB at 200M/6B |
|---|---:|---:|
| The target's own aggregate | 0.811 | 0.822 |
| Highest-SNR single task | 0.520 (SciQ, SNR 22.8) | 0.513 (BBC News, SNR 24.0) |
| Mean of the 5 highest-SNR tasks | 0.599 | |
| Best single task in hindsight | 0.784 (MT-MBPP R) | 0.771 (GitHub Python) |

On OBE Easy the highest-SNR task trails the aggregate by 29 points of decision accuracy, with a bootstrap 95% interval of -34 to -24 when I resample mixtures. The gap holds when the aggregate and the target share no tasks; with the 51 OBE Easy tasks split in half, one half at 160M against the other half at 200M/6B, it's 0.776 against 0.529. Noise in the target doesn't explain it either, since on the pairs that are clearly apart at 200M/6B (more than 3 SDs of a two-run difference) the aggregate goes up to 0.883 and SciQ stays at 0.523. Your `fits_reliability` SNRs are on the Qwen3 swarm over the 280 fit runs, so they differ from my 160M ones, and they put HellaSwag first among the OBE Easy tasks. As a lone pick HellaSwag gets 0.518, but your SNR-threshold subsets hold up well; the means of the SNR≥2, ≥5 and ≥8 tasks (49, 32 and 17 tasks) get 0.809, 0.799 and 0.773, close to the full aggregate. I reproduced your Spearman table and repeat SDs exactly, so I think we're reading the data the same way.

The ladder agrees, though it's an easy test; 14 of the 15 pairs are already more than 2 SDs apart at 3e18. The 3e18 aggregate orders all 15 the same way as 1e21, SciQ gets 7 and HellaSwag gets 1, and the MARINER and Olmix proposals were fit to those aggregates, so the aggregate has a head start there.

The rest I looked at after the planned test, so it's exploratory. A lot of the single-task gap is breadth; even at the same rung, SciQ orders only about 0.6 of pairs the same way as the 51-task average. Small-rung SNR doesn't say much about which tasks transfer to that average; across the 51 tasks its rank correlation with decision accuracy is 0.06 (0.28 against each task's own 200M/6B ranking), and SciQ and HellaSwag are near the bottom while the median task gets 0.69. SciQ doesn't agree with itself across the two rungs either; at 160M it orders only 0.57 of pairs the same way as SciQ at 200M/6B, while HellaSwag log-prob did that at 0.94 on DataDecide. My guess is that the 6B runs repeat the small buckets more and that shifts single tasks around, but I haven't checked it yet. The other pairings of your swarms look the same, with the aggregate against SciQ at 0.837 against 0.612 from 160M to Qwen3 360M and 0.697 against 0.494 from Qwen3 360M to 200M/6B.

So on your mixtures, as on DataDecide, one task picked for low noise doesn't stand in for the average of all the BPBs (which is also the mean of log-probs here), while SNR-filtered averages like yours stay close to it. If we want fewer evals, filtering by SNR inside an average looks safe, and going down to one or two tasks probably needs them picked by agreement with a larger rung, which I haven't tested. Happy to share the plan and scripts if that's useful.

@Helw150, your GDsuite results on the same Delphi seed triples line up with the item-SE point in the original post; on its two-choice tasks the median seed SD is about 9 to 10 times the binomial item SE at both 1e21 and 1e22 (17 and 21 tasks, ranging from 0.6x to 82x), though the items are templated, so the binomial SE may be too small and I can't size that without the raw files. The README mentions per-item `raw/` files and I think only `summary.jsonl` made it to the Hub, so if those are easy to add for the six seed checkpoints I could run the paired version of this on them too. For the extra seeds, I know the uploads would need input/help based on #10758 (cc @RohithKuditipudi). If per-question eval outputs from those runs are easier to share than the weights, they'd already cover what I need here

_Edits: labeled the table (the numbers are decision accuracy, not SNR), described your SNR table and subsets properly, added the breadth, rung and ladder caveats, and stated the GDsuite ratio as a median._

comments.author: dbuddha
comments.body:
So after seeing Calvin's comment in discord, i went back through both of my posts here with an independent check of every number, every linked issue and the Marin eval code they describe, and edited them in place.

Mainly none of the reported numbers changed, but some of the framing was off, so I wanted to describe it here so its especially clear for any one reading this 
-  I had described #5247 as ending on the single-eval rule that Result 2 tests, but it picks the smooth proxy with the highest SNR for each task, so Result 2 tests a different rule that's closer to the fewer-evals idea. 
- In the swarm comment I only compared @Calvin-Xu's SNR ranking as a single pick, and his SNR-threshold subsets hold up well (0.809, 0.799 and 0.773 for SNR≥2, ≥5 and ≥8, against 0.811 for the full average), so filtering by SNR inside an average looks fine and it's the single pick that breaks.

I also added two caveats to the swarm comment. A lot of the single-task gap is breadth, since even at the same rung SciQ orders only about 0.6 of pairs the same way as the 51-task average, and 200M/6B has 5x the tokens and half the learning rate, so it tests repetition as much as scale. In the original post I softened claims that three seeds can't support; the Delphi ratio drop from about 4x to 1x isn't significant (p about 0.1), the MMLU accuracy ratio of 1.3 is within noise, the GDsuite 9 to 10x is a median, and the DataDecide hindsight tie doesn't hold when deciding at 150M. Thanks Calvin for catching the table label, it made me check the above as a good measure too

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

[#11866](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11866) (hinted tasks), [#11867](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11867) (fit), and the required [Delphi gate #11868](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11868) are open with no reported results, so the hero matrix cannot start yet. The [Hero export guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/README.md#L50-L58) says the pinned Marin vLLM wheel rejects schema 3 exports; serving parity is a second gate.

**Relevant code**
- [`export_cpu.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/export_cpu.py) — CPU export and shape validation.
- [`ops/vibe_check`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/vibe_check) — native Hero sampling.

# Proposed Fix

1. Once #11866, #11867, and #11868 pass, pin their revisions and results. Record each checkpoint URI, training `config.yaml` and metadata digest, tokenizer revision, exporter revision, serving wheel revision, seeds, eval protocol, and output root before submitting jobs.
2. Export d512 first with its recorded `GrugModelConfig`. Check the completed export manifest and every expected tensor shape. Serve it as a base model on `marin-vllm-gpu-20261118` and compare greedy completions against native JAX on about 20 fixed prompts. If the wheel rejects schema 3, use the JAX sampler for the ladder and record that protocol choice for every rung.
3. Run d512's GSM8K and MATH-500 matrix at both hint methods and all 11 H levels, using #11866's rollout counts. Publish its per-H curves before committing to the remaining five rungs. If both methods and both tasks remain flat within bootstrap uncertainty across H, halve the remaining rollout counts as specified in this issue.
4. Run d768, its twin, d1024, d1536, and held-out d2048 with the same pinned protocol. Store sample identities, hint method and level, reference ID, checkpoint, seed, and per-H aggregates in evalrecords. Use the d768 twin to report run-to-run noise.
5. Score Mochi step-390251 at H=0 on GSM8K and MATH-500 with the 64-GB200 native sampler and the same answer grading protocol. Run the two drift checkpoints only if the main fit is informative. Publish run IDs, per-H results, Mochi scores, uncertainty, and accelerator cost on this issue.

The full matrix waits on the Delphi gate and d512 validation. A concrete code defect found at either gate should get an issue-linked PR.

| Base-d1024 | `rav-ladder-d1024` | `store_81e7e39a` | B | 2048 | 0.0144 | 15,276 |
| Base-d1536 | `rav-ladder-d1536` | `store_81e7e39a` | B | 6144 | 0.0149 | 15,128 |
| Base-d2048 | `rav-ladder-d2048-v3` | `store_81e7e39a` | B, first phase only | 11264 | 0.0134 | 15,000 of 20,072 |
| Mix25-d512 to d1536 | `h100-mix25-20260912-d*` | `store_4d2e363d` | A first phase, then #9126's `main` from 25% and `cooldown` from 80% | 1024 | 0.0263 to 0.0061 | 3,930 to 90,767 |

Mixture A is the pair of phase weights that #8452 put into `harrier_mix_2026_08_18.json` on Aug 19; its first phase is the current `initial`. Mixture B is `harrier_mix_2026_08_17_1.json`, which that file carried before #8452. Both switch to their second phase at about 80% of steps. Between A and B, the total-variation distance over the 200 cell weights is 0.204 in the first phase and 0.405 in the second. Within each family the weights are identical. `store_4d2e363d` rebuilds `store_81e7e39a` with 16 sources exempt from fuzzy dedup (#8427). The twin and Base-d768 have identical `model` and `optimizer` configs; their other differences are hardware, expert and replica axes, and eval batch. All ten runs carry the same W&B tag, `harrier-mix-2026.08.18`.

ClassicLarry noted in #8435 that the hero's data mixture changed on Aug 19 from the one the scaling ladder used. The two H100 Base runs date from Aug 24 and use the newer mixture and store.

1. The twin's gap to Base-d768 contains this recipe change as well as run-to-run noise, so in expectation it overstates the noise. #9126 has one measurement of that gap before any mixture switch: Mix25-d768, which has the twin's configuration up to its switch at step 2,880, was 0.61% lower in macro BPB than the GB200 d768 rung at 20% of training. None of the released rungs has a second run of the same recipe, so a noise floor for #11870 needs another run or another source.
2. Fit Base within one family, or estimate the A-to-B offset from the d768 pair and correct for it. Base-d512 exists only in family A, so a d512-to-d1536 fit puts its smallest rung on the other recipe. The held-out Base-d2048 point at step 15,000 is before its second-phase switch at step 16,032, so it differs from the other rungs in mixture as well as in schedule progress. Per `docs/reports/hero-mixture-log.md`, Mochi trained on `store_4d2e363d` starting from `initial`, so family A matches Mochi's first phase; the family B mixtures match none of the three phases in that log.
3. For the #11563 fits on the #12230 checkpoints: Base and Mix25 at d1024 and d1536 also differ in batch (2048 and 6144 against 1024), peak LR (0.0144 and 0.0149 against 0.0102 and 0.0061) and Adam beta2 (0.95 against 0.968), at equal token counts. At d512 and d768, the H100 Base runs and Mix25 differ only in the mixture schedule.

issues.body:
### Summary
An unparseable candidate must grade 0, failing closed, and never crash the grader into an infrastructure failure. A live attempt shows the crash class still reaching production through a shipped grader: `/tests/grade.py` exited 1 with reward NULL and the attempt typed `GRADER_INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILURE` because `reasoning_gym.arithmetic.prime_factorization._normalize_answer` raised `ValueError` from `int()` on a prose candidate.

### Observed failure
- Attempt: job 8878689 (difficulty Small solver). Reward: NULL. Verdict type: `GRADER_INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILURE`.
- Mechanism: the pinned scorer's `_normalize_answer` (`reasoning_gym/arithmetic/prime_factorization.py` L55) does `int(factor.strip())` over the reply's `×`-separated factors; prose raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int()`. The task's `/tests/grade.py` does not catch it, so the grader exits nonzero and the attempt is scored as infrastructure failure instead of reward 0.0.

### Current main already fails closed (verified 2026-11-24)
Every live grading path routes scorer calls through `verifyit.modes.grade_reasoning_gym._score_candidate`, which catches `MALFORMED_REPLY_ERRORS` (including `ValueError`) and scores 0.0 while checking the entry's own answer still earns its reward, and the generated grade scripts (`reasoning_gym_grade.py`, Nemotron Ultra `reasoning_gym_grade.py`) call that function. Empirically on main `e1742c045`/`3279c897a4`: a prose `prime_factorization` candidate scores `0.0`, an empty one `0.01` (the scorer's own contract), the valid answer `1.0`. Behavior tests exist: `test_prime_factorization_prose_scores_zero_and_keeps_numeric_rewards`, `test_prime_factorization_bad_reference_is_an_invalid_task`. The guards landed in #11516 (2026-11-15) and #11937 (2026-11-21).

### Diagnosis
The failing job's shipped `/tests/grade.py` predates those guards — a deployed task package built from an earlier main. Frozen packages do not pick up scorer fixes until re-versioned.

### Asks
1. Identify the task package and version job 8878689 ran, confirm its `grade.py` predates the guards, and re-version the affected frozen selection so its grader picks up the fail-closed scorer.
2. A code-level defense at the last line of defense (weaverbot draft PR requested on this issue): the generated Reasoning Gym grade scripts should print `0.0` and exit 0 when the scorer raises on an unparseable candidate — verifying the entry's own answer still scores, so a broken entry stays an error — so a rebuilt package can never type an unparseable candidate `GRADER_INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILURE`, whatever exception a current or future scorer raises. Behavior tests: a prose candidate prints 0.0 with exit code 0, and a valid answer prints its real score.

Related: #11937 (malformed replies → 0.0 on main), #11990 (graded replies setting their own reward, fixed), #11516 (prime factors scored zero).

## Overview

This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” release of a 67B A2B MoE, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 24, 2026: 18 non-agentic benchmarks, 8 Harbor agentic benchmarks, and 4 reserved out-of-distribution benchmarks.

## Complete eval list, with hyperparameters

### Details on our Evals

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question in one run through the shared seeded-repeat implementation and scores the integer final answers.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA stratified (Loose).** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. The campaign uses Evalchemy's pinned `NUPA5K-Loose` benchmark: a deterministic 5,000-record stratified sample covering 44 tasks and 2,391 strata, scored with permissive answer extraction rather than the paper's direct-answer protocol.
- **SWE-bench Verified.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced the 500-task, human-validated repository-issue repair set. The campaign runs Harbor's canonical `swebench-verified@1.0` implementation with mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, one trial per issue, and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2, three trials per task, and reports mean verifier success across trials.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.1.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1` at ref 6 through Harbor, with three Terminus-2 trials per task, a 65,536-token context window, and a 16,384-token per-turn output cap.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** BixBench is a computational biology benchmark. The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Tau bench tests whether a model can reliably help someone complete a task from beginning to end. Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** SOTOPIA is a role-playing benchmark where the agent must assume a fictional character and pursue a goal in a simulated scenario, pitted against other agents. The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge. It linearly normalizes each of the seven official dimensions, averages them into an overall score, and applies a cohort-level response-length control. Normalized goal achievement remains available as a non-default diagnostic.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals, remove or modify ID evals if we think the results are broken, unintuitive or wrong (reporting the eval as modified)

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data, deliberately modify ID evals to favor our own models

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited), modify OOD evals

### How do we choose which model to release?

We track dozens of candidate checkpoints. Including every candidate in the baseline ranking would
make the critical-difference plot unreadable and would let the number of closely related Snowball
checkpoints bias the cohort. We therefore select one release checkpoint in an internal tournament,
then compare only that checkpoint with the baseline cohort.

The tournament includes every Snowball- or Grug-named candidate with a complete set of observed,
durably linked scores. It does not impute missing cells. FinanceBench and PIQA are excluded because
they did not discriminate reliably within this candidate cohort; TriviaQA is excluded because its
answer extractor proved overly sensitive to response format. The other 23 benchmarks receive equal
weight.

For each model pair and benchmark, let `d = score_a - score_b` and let `s_a` and `s_b` be the
task-level SEMs after multiplying each by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` for the infrastructure-failure tolerance.
The outcome is decisive only when `abs(d) > 1.96 * hypot(s_a, s_b)`. Its sign determines the winner;
otherwise the benchmark is a tie. A win is worth 1, a tie 0.5, and a loss 0. Each pairwise win rate
is the mean of those values across the 23 benchmarks. A candidate's tournament score is the
unweighted mean of its pairwise win rates against every other candidate. If candidates have exactly
the same tournament score, pooled benchmark win rate and then model ID break the tie.

The completed 21-model tournament selected
`open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10`, with a mean pairwise win rate of
0.627. This checkpoint is labeled **Snowball** in the baseline figures.

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. Almost all of our benchmarks use this.
- **`mc2`:** Probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768.
- **`length-controlled normalized overall score`:** SOTOPIA-hard's seven official dimensions are each linearly normalized to `[0, 1]`, then averaged per episode. Across the full comparison cohort, a fractional logistic GLM fits model, task, and `tanh`-transformed response-length effects. The reportable score predicts each episode at zero response-length difference from that task's cohort median, then averages those predictions. Length is the evaluated character's total emitted characters over the episode. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model. Normalized goal achievement is retained as an explicit non-default scoring mode.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. Unless a benchmark specifies another cap, multi-turn generation is limited to 8192 tokens per turn. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit. Ling Lite's native 32,768-token window uses `mrcr-32k.yaml`; the historical 65,536-token Snowball candidate uses `mrcr-65k.yaml`; every release-figure model uses `mrcr.yaml` otherwise.
- **τ³ context selection:** [The Qwen3.6 τ³ ablation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9743) selected 131,072 total context and 32,768 per-turn output (153/373 scoreable trials; estimated accuracy 0.410) as the optimal for this eval.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`.

### LLM judges

Five evals involve an LLM judge.

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers the deterministic check cannot establish. Empty extracted answers score zero before
  any judge request. The reported scores use the fixed-grader replay of sealed responses described
  below, rather than the initial judge labels in the generation jobs.
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** after each completed social interaction, the official episode evaluator
  scores believability, relationship, knowledge, secret keeping, social-rule compliance,
  financial and material benefit, and goal achievement. The verifier normalizes all seven
  dimensions and uses their mean as the default per-episode reward. Cohort analysis applies the
  response-length correction defined above; the judge does not perform that correction.
- **τ³-bench:** the verifier combines deterministic task checks with an LLM evaluator for
  natural-language assertions. The separately configured LLM that simulates the user is part of
  the task environment, not the judge.

Judge deployment is benchmark-specific:

- **FinanceBench** and **OlympiadBench** use locally hosted `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` at revision
  `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba` for their final offline regrades. The judge runs
  on eight H100s in RNO2A with tensor parallelism 8, a 262,144-token context window, and the
  `minimax_m3` reasoning parser. The request constrains the response to `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` with vLLM `structured_outputs.choice`; Evalchemy retains each benchmark's native
  prompt, parsing, deterministic checks, and score aggregation. The replay reads the already sealed
  model responses and changes only the judge deployment.
- **BixBench** uses a co-hosted `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` judge at revision
  `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`. Marin serves it on eight H100s with tensor
  parallelism 8, a 32,768-token context window, the `minimax_m3` reasoning parser, prefix
  caching, and CUDA graphs enabled. The verifier receives the co-hosted endpoint and model
  identity directly from Marin; it does not use the Together judge environment.
- **SOTOPIA-hard** uses `openai/gpt-oss-120b` through Together for both the fixed counterpart
  and the official episode evaluator. Its LiteLLM identifier is
  `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first segment selects the OpenAI-compatible provider and
  the remainder is Together's model ID.
- **τ³-bench** uses that same Together-hosted model and LiteLLM identifier for both the user
  simulator and the natural-language assertion evaluator. The two roles are independently
  configured even though this campaign pins them to the same checkpoint.

Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` escalates 128 → 512 → 2048 when a completion is
  empty. Both final replays deploy MiniMax with a 262,144-token judge context window and constrain
  the output to one of the three labels through the pinned vLLM request option. The raw completion
  and parsed label are retained for audit. The judge window deliberately exceeds the 73,664-token
  generation window because responses can expand when re-tokenized by MiniMax.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls the co-hosted MiniMax Chat Completions endpoint
  with `max_tokens=1024` and a structured response schema containing one boolean score.
  Sampling follows the endpoint's service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge. The verifier preserves
  all seven scores, the normalized overall reward, and the evaluated agent's emitted character
  count. `goal` may be selected explicitly for diagnostic runs, but is not the release default.
- **τ³ natural-language assertions:** the pinned τ³ adapter passes only assertions that need
  semantic evaluation to its configured LLM; deterministic assertions remain programmatic.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Thinking mode

The main table records the policy for every benchmark. `on` and `off` set
`enable_thinking` through the model or benchmark config; a benchmark override wins over the model
default. `model default` means the benchmark adds no override, and `not applicable` means the task
does not use a generated chat response. If a model cannot turn reasoning off (e.g. GPT-OSS), an `off` benchmark
uses the model's lowest available reasoning setting instead.

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

An evaluation may be sealed as soon as at least 90% of its declared trials have valid scores under
the campaign configuration. Up to 10% of declared trials may be absent because of infrastructure
failures; the result does not need to wait for those trials to be recovered. Reported uncertainty
must include this infrastructure-failure tolerance. Task-level outcomes, including agent timeouts
recorded as scores of zero, are scored trials rather than infrastructure failures.

#### Zero-score trace audit

A score of exactly zero shall be reported only after agent review of at least ten representative
traces, or every trace when the evaluation has fewer than ten. The review will check model output,
harness parsing, verifier output, and serving or sandbox errors and accept the zero when the traces support model or task failure and no untracked infrastructure failure explains the result. Otherwise, the result should be rejected and re-run under the policy.

#### Harbor

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

##### Ambiguous Harbor Errors

- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing scoreable work. We treat these errors as score-able but if a trial returns more than 30% NonZeroAgentExitCodeError the agent or human executing the policy should review the traces to look for infrastructure errors and invalidate the run if any are discovered.

#### Evalchemy

Under the current Evalchemy pin, `malformed_model_response` is the only named error category that
remains scoreable. It means the model endpoint returned a response that Evalchemy could not parse,
or returned no usable final-answer content. Evalchemy substitutes an empty generation, preserves
the diagnostic category, and lets the benchmark grade that generation normally.

`AgentTimeoutError`, `model_transport`, and `grader_infrastructure` are currently serialized with
the `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR` marker and excluded from scored coverage. They therefore count
against the 10% infrastructure-failure allowance rather than as zero-valued model outcomes. Other
task-level failures, including `generation_policy`, `generation`, `grading`, `serialization`,
`incomplete_evaluation`, and `invalid_result`, do not produce a scoreable trial.

This exposes a mismatch with the intended Evalchemy timeout rule below: the release policy says an
`AgentTimeoutError` should score `0.0`, but the current pinned implementation treats it as
infrastructure. Results and coverage from this pin must follow the recorded implementation behavior;
making Evalchemy timeouts scoreable requires a new code pin and provenance.

#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. The repository-owned campaign validator checks these values
before submission, so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models in terms of parameter count and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.

### Configuration immutability

For convenience, Marin packages a launcher for policy evals. The launcher must not alter model-serving settings or benchmark semantics (except model-specific chat templates and model-specific Harbor context and compaction values). It may resolve credentials, cluster placement, output locations, concurrency, and other operational values.

Each durable run record preserves the effective model configuration, evaluator configuration, code revision, and Harbor policy digest. Any other semantic change requires a new checked-in config and code revision.

## Eval launch commands (Marin)

These commands require access to the `marin` Iris controller and the `cw-rno2a` federated cluster.
Set `MARIN_DIR` to a clean checkout of the pinned campaign revision and `MODEL` to a filename stem under
the repository's campaign `model-configs/` directory. The launcher validates every pin and canonical config, resolves the
required credentials, snapshots the effective command and configs, and submits one shared-serving
root. It deliberately supplies no eval-policy label.

```bash
REPRO_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
git clone https://github.com/marin-community/marin.git "$REPRO_DIR/marin"
git -C "$REPRO_DIR/marin" checkout 75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a
```
